issues.legal_issue: Whether an agreement granting use of premises creates a lease or only a licence depends on the substance of the arrangement and the parties’ intention, rather than the document’s label or exclusive possession alone.
material_facts: The occupant was admitted temporarily to a member’s flat with the housing society’s permission and became a nominal member of the society.

The written agreement described the arrangement as a licence, granted use of the flat together with its furniture and fittings for a limited period, and stated that the occupant would not claim tenancy or sub-tenancy.
The occupant had exclusive possession, but the terms of the agreement and the surrounding circumstances showed an intention to permit temporary use without transferring an interest in the flat.
issues.conclusion: The agreement created a licence, not a lease.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease transfers a right to enjoy immovable property; section 52 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 describes a licence as a permission that does not create an interest in the property. The substance of the agreement and the parties’ intention, gathered from its terms and surrounding, antecedent and subsequent circumstances, control; exclusive possession is significant but not conclusive. The Court relied on Board of Revenue v. A.M. Ansari, Tarkeshwar Sio Thakur Jiu v. Dar Dass Dey & Co., and Sohan Lal Naraindas v. Laxmidas Raghunath Gadit, and considered N.E. Railway v. Hastings, Isaac v. Hotel De Paris Ltd. and Booker v. Palmer. It distinguished Antoniades v. Villiers, where the apparent licence terms were a pretence and the arrangement was intended to create a joint tenancy.

predicates.temporary_use_was_granted: The grantor permitted the occupant to use the premises temporarily, including with the associated furniture or fittings.
predicates.agreement_disclaimed_tenancy: The parties’ agreement stated that the occupant would not claim tenancy or sub-tenancy.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_showed_no_tran: The surrounding circumstances, including the occupant’s temporary admission and nominal membership, showed that the parties did not intend to transfer an interest in the premises.

issues.definition: When temporary use is granted, the agreement disclaims tenancy, and the surrounding circumstances show no transfer of interest, the arrangement is a licence rather than a lease.

issues.legal_issue: A licensee obtains deemed-tenant protection under the applicable rent legislation only if the licensee remains in occupation under a subsisting licence on the statutory eligibility date.
material_facts: The licence was terminated with effect from before the statutory eligibility date for deemed-tenant status.
The occupant remained in the flat after termination but was not occupying it under a subsisting licence on the eligibility date.
The occupant sought the protection available to licensees treated as tenants under the rent legislation.
issues.conclusion: The occupant was not entitled to deemed-tenant protection because the licence had ended before the eligibility date; the occupant could not rely on the rent legislation’s bar to the cooperative proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5(4A), 5(11)(bb) and 15A of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, read together, require occupation as a licensee under a subsisting licence on the relevant date. A person who remains after termination, withdrawal or revocation of the licence is not then a licensee for this purpose. The Court relied on D.H. Maniar v. Waman Laxman Kudav and O.N. Bhatnagar v. Smt. Rukibai Narsindas, and referred to Chandavarkar Sita Ratna Rao v. Ashalata S. Guram; it distinguished Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Shyam Cooperative Housing Society on its facts.

predicates.claim_for_deemed_tenant_protection: The occupant sought statutory protection on the basis of being treated as a tenant because of occupation as a licensee.
predicates.licence_ended_before_eligibility_date: The permission to occupy had been terminated before the date on which the occupant had to be occupying under a subsisting licence.

issues.definition: If an occupant seeks deemed-tenant protection but the licence ended before the eligibility date, the occupant is not entitled to that protection.

issues.legal_issue: A cooperative court may hear a cooperative housing society’s possession dispute against a nominal member where the dispute touches the society’s business and the occupant has no landlord-tenant relationship protected by rent legislation.
material_facts: A tenant co-partner member and the cooperative housing society brought a proceeding to recover possession from an occupant who had been admitted as a nominal member.
The occupant’s licence had been terminated before the statutory eligibility date, so the occupant did not qualify for deemed-tenant protection under the rent legislation.
The dispute concerned the occupant’s continued possession of premises in a tenant co-partnership cooperative housing society.
issues.conclusion: The possession dispute touched the business of the society, and the cooperative courts had jurisdiction; the rent legislation did not bar the proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Section 91 of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, covers qualifying disputes touching the business of a society between the parties described in that section. Section 28(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, does not bar such a proceeding where the parties do not stand in a landlord-tenant relationship protected by that Act. The Court relied on O.N. Bhatnagar v. Smt. Rukibai Narsindas and Smt. Krishna Rajpal Bhatia v. Miss Leela H. Advani, and considered Deccan Merchants Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. M/s Dalichand Jugraj Jain. It distinguished Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Shyam Cooperative Housing Society because the occupant there was protected under the rent legislation.

rule.if: cooperative_housing_possession_dispute and occupant_was_a_nominal_member and licence_ended_before_eligibility_date and dispute_concerned_society_business

predicates.cooperative_housing_possession_dispute: A cooperative housing society and a member brought a proceeding to recover premises from an occupant.
predicates.occupant_was_a_nominal_member: The occupant had been admitted as a nominal member of the cooperative society.
predicates.licence_ended_before_eligibility_date: The permission to occupy had been terminated before the date on which the occupant had to be occupying under a subsisting licence to obtain rent-law protection.
predicates.dispute_concerned_society_business: The dispute concerned possession of premises in the cooperative housing society and the society’s relationship with its member and occupant.

issues.definition: In a cooperative housing possession dispute, when the occupant is a nominal member, the licence ended before the eligibility date, and the dispute concerns the society’s business, the cooperative court has jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional challenge to the reach of the cooperative-dispute provision is not tenable when the challenger is a nominal member involved in a dispute touching the society’s business.
material_facts: The occupant had applied for and obtained nominal membership of the cooperative housing society in connection with permission to occupy a member’s flat.
The society and the member sought to recover possession in a dispute concerning the society’s business.
The occupant argued that the cooperative-dispute provision was unconstitutional insofar as it reached persons who were not society members.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional challenge was not tenable because the occupant was a nominal member involved in a dispute touching the society’s business.
issues.legal_principle: Section 91 of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, applies to specified disputes involving a society and persons within the categories identified in the section, including a person claiming membership. The Court rejected the challenge under Article 14 of the Constitution because the occupant was a nominal member and the dispute touched the society’s business; it relied on the application of section 91 to the dispute and the decisions in O.N. Bhatnagar v. Smt. Rukibai Narsindas and Smt. Krishna Rajpal Bhatia v. Miss Leela H. Advani.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_cooperative_: A party challenged the constitutional validity of the authority to hear a cooperative society’s dispute insofar as it reaches persons who are not ordinary members.
predicates.occupant_was_a_nominal_member: The occupant had applied for and obtained nominal membership of the cooperative society in connection with occupation of its premises.
predicates.dispute_concerned_society_business: The dispute concerned recovery of premises in the society and the relationship between the society, its member and the occupant.

issues.definition: When a party challenges cooperative dispute authority, but the occupant is a nominal member and the dispute concerns the society’s business, the challenge is not tenable.
